chunks: Stack versus heap. The question: What is the difference between the stack and the heap?
The stack and the heap are two parts of RAM that hold data created while a program runs. The stack is for function calls. It is automatic, very fast, small and fixed in size.
The heap is for data that must outlive a call or whose size is unknown until the program runs. You ask for a piece and give it back yourself.
The heap is flexible but slower, and it can leak or fragment. Small chips in gadgets therefore use the stack and fixed buffers wherever they can.
The stack is a pile of papers on your desk. You add each new one on top, and you always remove the top one first. The heap is a parking lot.
Cars stay as long as their owners want, and they leave in any order. After many cars come and go, empty spaces are scattered.
A bus may not fit even when plenty of spaces are empty in total.
Code and globals are fixed at link time. The stack and heap are the two regions that change size at runtime, growing toward each other from opposite ends of the free RAM.
On a desktop, virtual memory makes the gap huge; on a microcontroller it may be a few hundred bytes.
Stack: memory for function calls. It is freed automatically, newest first. Heap: memory you request and release yourself, in any order.
malloc / free: the C calls that request a heap block and give it back. Memory leak: a heap block you never freed and can no longer use.
Fragmentation: free memory split into pieces too small to use. Memory pool: a set of equal-size blocks reused with no fragmentation.
Allocating on the stack is one subtraction from the stack pointer (the number marking the top of the stack), and returning undoes it. A heap block needs a search for free space.
Picture a 1,000-byte heap holding ten 100-byte blocks, all in use. Free the five odd-numbered blocks.
Now 500 bytes are free, but the biggest hole is only 100 bytes, so malloc(200) fails. That is the whole idea.
"The stack holds function-call frames: locals and return addresses.
It's allocated by moving the stack pointer, freed automatically on return, fast and cache friendly, but small and strictly LIFO.
The heap holds data that has to outlive a call or has a runtime-determined size.
It's allocated with malloc and freed explicitly, so it's flexible but slower and can leak or fragment.
In embedded I prefer stack and static allocation because the heap can fail unpredictably in the field."
